# Maser and laser (`laser`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: needs quantum_mechanics, electromagnetic_waves_radio; helped by radar, glass_mirrors, semiconductors_transistor
- Core idea: An atom in an excited state, struck by light of exactly the frequency it would emit, emits a second wave in step with the first and in the same direction (stimulated emission). If more atoms are in the upper state than in the lower, which never happens in heat equilibrium and must be forced by pumping with a flash lamp, an electric discharge or a current, light passing through is amplified instead of absorbed. Put the material between two parallel mirrors, one of them slightly transparent, and the light that runs along the axis builds up into a narrow beam of a single colour, with all waves in step. First done with microwaves in ammonia gas (maser), then with a ruby rod and a flash lamp, and with a helium-neon discharge tube.
- Pitfalls:
  - Trying to get the inversion by heating; heat always leaves more atoms in the lower state, so a separate pump and at least three energy levels are needed
  - Mirrors that are not parallel to a few seconds of arc, so that no beam builds up
  - Eye damage: even a weak beam is focused by the eye onto a point of the retina, and the harm is instant and permanent
  - Imagining a death ray; the early uses are measurement, alignment, surgery on the retina, and later communication through glass fibre
- History: europe: 1916–1917 – Einstein derives stimulated emission; 1939 Fabrikant (Moscow) proposes amplification by an inverted medium; 1954–1955 Basov and Prokhorov's maser theory (Moscow); americas: 1954 – ammonia maser of Gordon, Zeiger and Townes (Columbia); 1957–1958 Schawlow and Townes's paper on optical masers and Gould's notebook, which coins the word laser (the patent fight lasted thirty years); May 1960 Maiman's ruby laser (Hughes); December 1960 helium-neon laser of Javan, Bennett and Herriott (Bell Labs); 1962 semiconductor laser (Hall, General Electric)
- Read:
  - A. L. Schawlow & C. H. Townes, Infrared and Optical Masers, Physical Review 112 (1958)
  - Jeff Hecht, Beam: The Race to Make the Laser (2005)
  - Charles H. Townes, How the Laser Happened: Adventures of a Scientist (1999)
